title: “HERE I AM, SEND ME” SOUNDS INSPIRING—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT GOD SENT ISAIAH TO DO
paragraphs: “HERE I AM, SEND ME” SOUNDS INSPIRING—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT GOD SENT ISAIAH TO DO

We turned Isaiah’s terrifying surrender into an inspirational slogan. But God never promised Isaiah applause, influence, crowds, or visible success. He sent him to speak truth to people who would keep hearing—and still refuse to listen. And that changes what “Here I am” means for every one of us.
It looks beautiful on a T-shirt.
It fits perfectly beneath a photograph of mountains, an open Bible, or someone standing with arms raised during worship.
The kind of sentence Christians love to quote when talking about purpose, calling, ministry, and doing something great for God.
But there is something we rarely put on the shirt.
Something we often leave out of the sermon.
Something uncomfortable waiting immediately after Isaiah says those famous words.
Isaiah volunteered before he knew where God was sending him.
And when God finally told him what the assignment would look like, it was nothing like the version of “calling” many of us secretly hope for.
No promise of a massive audience.
No guarantee that people would celebrate his message.
No assurance that his ministry would look successful.
Instead, God sent Isaiah to a people who would hear truth and resist it.
People who could listen without surrendering.
People who could see without truly perceiving.
People whose spiritual condition had become so hardened that Isaiah’s preaching would expose just how deeply they had refused God.
And Isaiah asked the question almost anyone would have asked:
there would still be a stump.
There would still be a holy seed.
There would still be hope after judgment.
doesn’t sound like a motivational quote anymore.
And maybe that is exactly why we need to read Isaiah 6 again.
Because before Isaiah ever said, “Send me,” he saw Someone.
“In the year that King Uzziah died,” Isaiah says, “I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up.”
But the throne of heaven was not empty.
Isaiah sees the Lord exalted, the temple filled with His glory, and seraphim crying to one another:
“Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.”
And notice what Isaiah does not say.
“This is amazing. I finally discovered my purpose.”
He does not ask for a platform.
He does not start thinking about his ministry brand.
He collapses beneath the awareness of his own sinfulness.
That is where the real “Here I am” begins.
Isaiah sees God more clearly, and suddenly Isaiah sees Isaiah more clearly.
“I am a man of unclean lips.”
There is something painfully recognizable about that.
We spend enormous amounts of energy protecting the version of ourselves we want other people to see.
We know how to look okay.
We know which photographs to post.
We can raise our hands while protecting our idols.
Say “God first” while giving Him whatever remains after everything else has consumed us.
We can look spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
And all the filters stop working.
Isaiah does not compare himself with the people around him.
And comparison becomes meaningless when holiness becomes the standard.
Maybe that is why genuine encounters with God produce humility rather than spiritual arrogance.
The closer Isaiah gets to holiness, the less impressed he becomes with himself.
But this is where Isaiah 6 becomes breathtaking.
but He does not abandon him in his exposure.
One of the seraphim takes a burning coal from the altar and touches Isaiah’s mouth.
The very lips Isaiah confessed as unclean become the place where cleansing is applied.
“thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.”
In the Hebrew text of Isaiah 6:7 we read:
The sense is powerful: your guilt has departed; your sin has been atoned for.
Isaiah does not earn his way from “Woe is me” to “Send me.”
That pattern reaches its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that dirty people can make themselves clean if they become religious enough.
The Gospel is that the Holy One came for sinners.

Jesus Christ lived without the sin that condemns us, gave Himself for sinners at the cross, and rose again. Forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance. Reconciliation with God is received through Christ.
Before “send me” comes the God who saves.
That matters because some of us have spent years trying to serve God while secretly attempting to pay Him back.
The cross is not God lending you salvation until your ministry becomes impressive enough to deserve it.
Christ saves sinners who could never save themselves.
And only after Isaiah’s guilt has been dealt with does he hear the question:
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
Not merely, “I happen to be standing here.”
It is the language of availability.
No request to preview the assignment.
No question about whether this calling will make him admired.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 6:9 carries that terrible repetition:
שִׁמְעוּ שָׁמוֹעַ וְאַל־תָּבִינוּ וּרְאוּ רָאוֹ וְאַל־תֵּדָעוּ
Shim'u shamoa ve'al-tavinu; ure'u ra'o ve'al-teda'u.
This is not a picture of people who lacked exposure to truth.
It is a warning about what can happen when truth is repeatedly encountered and repeatedly resisted.
And that should frighten those of us who have spent years around Christianity.
Because there is a difference between hearing sermons and hearing God.
There is a difference between knowing Christian vocabulary and knowing Christ.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
You can know worship lyrics by heart.
You can even tell other people what they need to repent of.
And still have rooms inside your own heart where Jesus is not welcome.
That is one of the terrifying implications of Isaiah’s commission.
Exposure does not automatically produce surrender.

Jesus Himself later invokes Isaiah’s words when explaining the spiritual blindness surrounding His own ministry, and Isaiah 6 appears again in the New Testament in connection with people hearing divine truth without truly receiving it.
So perhaps the question is not simply:
Perhaps another question needs to follow:
“What have I done with what I heard?”
Because maybe you already know what God has been confronting.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The addiction you renamed a “struggle” because calling it bondage became uncomfortable.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible gathering dust while your screen-time keeps climbing.
The person you refuse to forgive while asking God daily to forgive you.
The compromise you once hated that now barely bothers you.
The conviction you keep postponing because you assume there will always be another Sunday.
One of the most dangerous things that can happen to a human heart is not that God never speaks.
It is becoming comfortable hearing Him while refusing to respond.
Isaiah’s story refuses to let us confuse familiarity with faithfulness.
You can almost feel the weight inside those words.
How long do I preach when people refuse to listen?
How long do I remain faithful when nothing appears to be changing?
How long do I obey when obedience seems fruitless?
How long do I keep telling the truth when people would rather have something easier?
But perhaps you have whispered your own version.
How long do I keep praying for my child?
How long do I keep loving this family when nobody understands why I follow Jesus?
How long do I keep choosing integrity when dishonesty seems to get rewarded?
How long do I keep serving when nobody notices?
How long do I keep sharing Christ when people laugh?
How long do I keep believing when I cannot see what God is doing?
Isaiah was not commissioned to control the response.
We have become obsessed with measurable success.
And those things can sometimes tell us useful things, but they cannot finally determine whether a servant has been faithful.
Sometimes obedience produces visible fruit quickly.
Sometimes you plant what another person will water.
Sometimes you speak words someone will remember years later.
Sometimes you remain faithful in a place where almost nobody applauds.
The servant does not control the harvest.
And then, buried inside a chapter filled with holiness, judgment, blindness, devastation, and loss, comes a strange image.
Judgment would not have the final word.
Isaiah would later speak astonishing words about a coming child, a coming King, a servant who would suffer, and good news proclaimed to the broken.
And centuries later, John’s Gospel would look back at Isaiah’s vision and connect Isaiah’s encounter with glory to Christ.
The story was always moving toward Jesus.
all of it drives us toward our desperate need for redemption.
Maybe you began reading this because “Here I am, send me” sounded inspiring.
But perhaps God is asking something deeper than whether you are willing to go somewhere dramatic.
Maybe the first place He wants truth to reach is you.
Because “send me” without “woe is me” can become ambition wearing Christian clothing.
And “woe is me” without grace becomes despair.
But Isaiah gives us the Gospel-shaped movement:
And faithfulness belongs to God even when the assignment hurts.
Maybe your “Here I am” tonight is not boarding an airplane for another country.
Maybe it is finally confessing what you have hidden.
Maybe it is opening your Bible again.
Maybe it is asking someone to pray for you.
Maybe it is returning to church.
Maybe it is ending the compromise.
Maybe it is telling the truth.
Maybe it is sharing Jesus with the person whose name has been sitting in your heart for months.
Maybe it is simply getting on your knees and saying:
“Jesus, I have heard You so many times.
Please do not let me become someone who can hear truth without obeying it.
If that prayer exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this into another article you read, felt for thirty seconds, and forgot.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that faithfulness is never wasted in the hands of God.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because an algorithm is holy. It isn't.
Send it privately to someone who has been drifting.
Even send it to the person who does not believe yet but is willing to wrestle honestly with Jesus.
Because there may come a day when you will need to remember that God never promised every assignment would feel successful.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront compromise, understand the Gospel, and keep your eyes on Jesus, follow this ministry and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
There is also a deeper way to partner with this work.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel work continue.
Think of it not as purchasing access to God, but as partnership.
Participation in spreading the message of grace.
If you can support the work, thank you.
If you cannot, you can still pray.
You can still help place truth in front of another human soul.
You can still whisper the words Isaiah whispered thousands of years ago.
Only now you know what those words can cost.
They are not a request for adventure.
They are surrender before the assignment is revealed.
“Send me when all I can see is a stump.”
Because sometimes the evidence that God is working is not a forest.
it is one stubborn stump in devastated ground,
with a holy seed still alive inside it.
And maybe that is where you are right now.
Wondering whether God has forgotten the story He started in you.
The stump is not the end when God still holds the seed.
Jesus Christ still calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus Christ still takes people with unclean lips, cleanses them by grace, and sends them carrying truth into a world that may not want to hear it.
do not answer because the assignment looks glamorous.
Do not answer because you expect applause.
Do not answer because you think serving Him will make you important.
Look at the holiness that exposes you.
Look at the grace that cleanses you.
Look at the cross where Christ gave Himself for sinners.
Then answer because the One who calls you is worthy.
if the road becomes harder than you imagined...
if faithfulness costs more than the inspirational quote ever warned you...

The most powerful “Here I am” is not spoken by the person who knows where God will send them—it is spoken by the person who has seen enough of His grace to trust Him before knowing where the road goes.
